questions.title: The two-sided limit that disappears because the one-sided limits disagree
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.1 (introduction to the concept of a limit; one-sided limits and limits that do not exist)
questions.subtopic: 5.1 Introduction to the concept of a limit
questions.challenge_mechanism: The two-sided limit is denied entirely because the right-hand limit of 2 and the left-hand limit of -2 are unequal, so the function has no overall limit at x=1.
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{|x-1|}$ defined for all real $x$ except $x=1$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why $f(1)$ cannot be evaluated directly, and state what this means for the value of the function at $x=1$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For $x>1$, show that $f(x)$ simplifies to $x+1$ and hence state the right-hand limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $1$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For $x<1$, show that $f(x)$ simplifies to $-(x+1)$ and hence state the left-hand limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $1$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine whether the two-sided limit $\lim_{x\to 1}f(x)$ exists, justifying your answer using the one-sided limits.

questions.answer:
(a) Substituting $x=1$ gives $f(1)=\frac{0}{0}$, which is undefined because division by zero is not permitted **(M1)**, so the function has no value at that point **(A1)** and cannot be evaluated by direct substitution **(A1)**. A zero denominator means the algebraic expression has no numerical value at $x=1$, so the formula breaks down exactly where the limit is investigated **(R1)**. The expression therefore fails precisely because the denominator vanishes there.

(b) For $x>1$ the quantity $x-1$ is strictly positive, so $|x-1|=x-1$ and $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1$ **(M1)(A1)**. As $x$ tends to $1$ from above, this linear expression tends to $2$, so the right-hand limit is $2$ **(A1)(AG)**. The factor $x-1$ cancels legitimately because it is never zero on this side of $1$, leaving a well behaved linear function. This is why the one-sided limit exists even though the formula is undefined at the point.

(c) For $x<1$ the quantity $x-1$ is negative, so $|x-1|=-(x-1)$ and $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{-(x-1)}=-(x+1)$ **(M1)(A1)**. As $x$ tends to $1$ from below, $-(x+1)$ tends to $-2$, so the left-hand limit is $-2$ **(A1)(AG)**. The minus sign is forced by the absolute value on the negative side, because the denominator equals the opposite of the numerator factor. The left-hand limit therefore exists as a finite value distinct from the right-hand one.

(d) A two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits agree **(M1)**. Here the right-hand limit is $2$ and the left-hand limit is $-2$ **(A1)**, and since $2\neq -2$ **(A1)**, the two-sided limit does not exist **(R1)**. The unequal one-sided limits are exactly what prevent the overall limit from existing, because a proper limit must approach the same value from both directions.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for recognising that substituting $x=1$ produces $0/0$ and that division by zero is forbidden, (A1) for stating the expression is undefined, (A1) for noting the function has no value at $x=1$, and (R1) for the conclusion that direct evaluation fails and says nothing about the surrounding limit. 

(b) The (M1) is for using $|x-1|=x-1$ when $x>1$ and cancelling the common factor to reach $x+1$; the (A1) is for that simplified linear form. The second (A1) with (AG) is for the right-hand limit $2$, awarded only when the limit is explicitly evaluated as $x\to1^{+}$. Follow through from a different but consistent simplification is allowed.

(c) The (M1) is for the negative absolute value $|x-1|=-(x-1)$ when $x<1$ and the simplification to $-(x+1)$; the (A1) is for that form. The (A1)(AG) pair is for the left-hand limit $-2$. The minus sign is the most common omission and must be present for the mark.

(d) Award (M1) for the criterion that one-sided limits must agree, (A1) for quoting both limits $2$ and $-2$, (A1) for the inequality $2\neq-2$, and (R1) for concluding the two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.explanation: This item targets the first genuine stumbling block in the limit concept: a two-sided limit requires both sides to approach the same value, and here they do not. The function is built around an absolute value, so its algebraic form genuinely changes at $x=1$, and the candidate must treat the two sides separately rather than substitute once and hope. The intended route is to recognise that $|x-1|$ equals $x-1$ above $1$ and $-(x-1)$ below $1$, factor $x^{2}-1$ as $(x-1)(x+1)$, cancel, and read the two one-sided limits as $2$ and $-2$. The final conceptual step is the key: because the two limits differ, the two-sided limit does not exist, and many students wrongly declare it to be $0$ or to equal the undefined value at the point itself. The classic wrong turn is to cancel the factor $x-1$ without considering the sign of the absolute value, which produces the single value $x+1$ and hides the left-hand limit entirely. Another common error is to evaluate $f(1)$ as something like $0$ and to claim the limit is $0$ because the numerator vanishes. The numbers were chosen so the two one-sided limits are clean integers, $2$ and $-2$, that are obviously unequal, making the non-existence of the two-sided limit unambiguous. The absolute value is the lever: it is what forces the split into two cases, and a candidate who ignores it cannot reach the correct answer no matter how carefully they compute. The whole point is the disagreement of the one-sided limits, and the absolute value is the device that produces it.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.1 bullet introducing the concept of a limit, including one-sided limits and limits that do not exist. The lever is the absolute value in the denominator of f(x)=(x^2-1)/|x-1|, which forces the one-sided limits to be computed separately; the numbers were chosen so that for x>1 the function simplifies to x+1 giving a right-hand limit of 2, and for x<1 it simplifies to -(x+1) giving a left-hand limit of -2, making the two-sided limit fail unambiguously because 2 is not equal to -2. The item is not a reskin because the disagreement of the one-sided limits is the explicit object of the final part rather than a by-product of a routine evaluation.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the undefined form 0/0 at x=1, the simplification x+1 for x>1 giving a right-hand limit of 2, the simplification -(x+1) for x<1 giving a left-hand limit of -2, and the inequality 2 is not -2 confirming the two-sided limit does not exist, together with the numerical checks at x=1.001 and x=0.999.
solution_skeleton: split the definition at the point where the modulus changes sign
evaluate the left-hand and right-hand limits separately
compare the one-sided limits to decide whether the two-sided limit exists
discuss continuity and whether the discontinuity could be removed

questions.title: The cubic whose derivative flips sign twice
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.2 (increasing and decreasing functions; interpretation of f'(x))
questions.challenge_mechanism: The derivative factorises as 3(x-3)(x+1) and changes sign twice, so the cubic rises, falls and rises again with a local maximum and a local minimum at the two roots.
questions.question: Consider the cubic function $f(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}-9x+5$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By differentiating the cubic term by term, show that $f'(x)=3(x-3)(x+1)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the intervals on which $f$ is increasing and the intervals on which $f$ is decreasing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point at $x=-1$ and state its nature.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point at $x=3$ and state its nature.

questions.answer:
(a) Differentiating term by term using the power rule gives $f'(x)=3x^{2}-6x-9$ **(M1)**, which factors as $3(x^{2}-2x-3)$ **(A1)** and then as $3(x-3)(x+1)$ because $-3$ and $1$ sum to $-2$ and multiply to $-3$ **(A1)(AG)**. Expanding $3(x-3)(x+1)$ returns $3x^{2}-6x-9$, confirming the factorisation is correct **(R1)**. The derivative is therefore confirmed in a fully factored form that exposes its roots directly. This factorised shape is what makes the later sign analysis straightforward.

(b) The derivative is zero at $x=-1$ and $x=3$, which split the real line into three intervals **(M1)**, and its sign is positive outside these roots and negative between them **(A1)**. Hence $f$ is increasing on $x<-1$ and on $x>3$, and decreasing on $-1<x<3$ **(A1)(A1)**. The sign change is read directly from the factored form $3(x-3)(x+1)$ by testing the sign of each linear factor. The function therefore rises, then falls, then rises again.

(c) Substituting $x=-1$ into the original function gives $f(-1)=(-1)^{3}-3(1)-9(-1)+5=-1-3+9+5=10$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the stationary point is $(-1,10)$ **(A1)**. Since the derivative changes from positive to negative as $x$ passes $-1$, the point is a local maximum **(R1)**. The stationary point is therefore a peak on the curve at that coordinate.

(d) Substituting $x=3$ gives $f(3)=27-27-27+5=-22$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the stationary point is $(3,-22)$ **(A1)**. Since the derivative changes from negative to positive as $x$ passes $3$, the point is a local minimum **(R1)**. The stationary point is therefore a trough, and the cubic has completed its rise-fall-rise pattern. The steep drop of 32 units between the two turning points is a direct consequence of the positive leading coefficient and is easily understated.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the derivative $3x^{2}-6x-9$, (A1) for factoring out $3$ to reach $3(x^{2}-2x-3)$, and (A1)(AG) for the fully factored $3(x-3)(x+1)$. The (R1) is for verifying by expansion or by quoting the sum and product of the roots. A candidate who expands correctly but does not factor earns only the (M1).

(b) The (M1) is for the two roots $x=-1$ and $x=3$. The (A1) is for the correct sign pattern, and the two final (A1) marks are for the increasing intervals $x<-1$ and $x>3$ and the decreasing interval $-1<x<3$. Accept interval notation with or without the endpoints included.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=-1$, (A1) for the $y$-value $10$, (A1) for the point $(-1,10)$, and (R1) for identifying it as a local maximum from the sign change of $f'$. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting $x=3$, (A1) for $-22$, (A1) for the point $(3,-22)$, and (R1) for local minimum. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed provided the nature matches the sign change.
questions.explanation: This item is a standard but unforgiving exercise in reading the sign of a derivative. The cubic is chosen so that its derivative is a clean quadratic that factorises into $3(x-3)(x+1)$, giving two stationary points at $x=-1$ and $x=3$. The intended route is to differentiate, factor, locate the roots, then test the sign of the derivative in the three resulting intervals to decide where the function rises and falls. The point of the question is the double sign change: because the leading coefficient of $f$ is positive, the cubic eventually rises on both ends, so it must rise, fall and rise again, producing a local maximum followed by a local minimum. The classic wrong turn is to mis-factor the quadratic, for example writing $3(x-1)(x+3)$ with the constant in the wrong place, which moves the stationary points and inverts the intervals. Another error is to test the sign of $f'$ only at one point and assume the whole side behaves the same, missing the second root entirely. Candidates also confuse the nature of the stationary points, calling $x=-1$ a minimum because its $x$-value is smaller, or swapping the two $y$-values when stating the coordinates. The $y$-values $10$ and $-22$ were chosen so that the two stationary points are simple integers, and the factored form makes the sign chart immediate once the roots are found. The lever is the clean double sign change, which rewards a candidate who reasons from the factored derivative rather than from scattered point evaluations, and the steep drop between the two turning points is the feature most often understated.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.2 bullet on increasing and decreasing functions and the interpretation of f'(x). The lever is a cubic whose derivative factorises exactly as 3(x-3)(x+1), chosen so that it has two real roots at x=-1 and x=3 and therefore changes sign twice, giving a local maximum at (-1,10) and a local minimum at (3,-22); the coefficients -3 and -9 were selected so that the factorisation is clean and the stationary y-values are small integers. The item is not a reskin because the double sign change and the requirement to state the nature of both stationary points from the sign pattern are the core demands, not merely finding the derivative.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the derivative 3x^2-6x-9, its factorisation 3(x-3)(x+1), the two roots x=-1 and x=3, the y-values f(-1)=10 and f(3)=-22, and the gradient at x=1 which is 3-6-9=-12.
solution_skeleton: differentiate the cubic and find its critical points
use the sign of the derivative to determine the intervals of increase and decrease
classify each critical point with a sign table or the second derivative
sketch the curve using the stationary points and the intercepts

questions.title: The derivative that keeps a negative power
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.3 (derivative of f(x)=ax^n is f'(x)=anx^{n-1}, n in Z; negative integer powers included)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The term 2/x^3 differentiates to the negative power -6x^{-4}, so the gradient at x=2 is a fractional subtraction that must be evaluated exactly as 75.625.
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=3x^{4}-5x^{2}+\frac{2}{x^{3}}-7$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By applying the power rule to each term, show that $f'(x)=12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the gradient of the curve at $x=1$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the gradient of the curve at $x=2$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the gradient of the curve at $x=-1$ and determine whether $f$ is increasing or decreasing there.

questions.answer:
(a) Writing $\frac{2}{x^{3}}=2x^{-3}$, the power rule gives $\frac{d}{dx}(3x^{4})=12x^{3}$, $\frac{d}{dx}(-5x^{2})=-10x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(2x^{-3})=-6x^{-4}$, while the constant $-7$ differentiates to zero **(M1)(A1)**. Adding these three pieces yields $f'(x)=12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$ **(A1)(AG)**. The negative power remains because the index of $2x^{-3}$ drops from $-3$ to $-4$ when differentiated **(R1)**. The derivative is therefore confirmed with the negative power retained rather than converted back to a fraction. This is the form that must be used for every later substitution.

(b) Substituting $x=1$ into the derivative gives $f'(1)=12(1)-10(1)-6(1)=12-10-6=-4$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the gradient at $x=1$ is $-4$ **(A1)**. The value is negative because the $-6$ term dominates the other two contributions at this point **(R1)**. The gradient is therefore $-4$, meaning the curve is sloping downwards as it passes through $x=1$.

(c) Substituting $x=2$ gives $f'(2)=12(8)-10(2)-6(2^{-4})=96-20-\frac{6}{16}=76-0.375=75.625$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the gradient at $x=2$ is $75.625$ **(A1)**. The fractional subtraction must be carried through exactly, since $6/16=0.375$, to reach this precise decimal **(R1)**. The gradient is therefore $75.625$, a steep positive slope that contrasts sharply with the negative slope at $x=1$.

(d) Substituting $x=-1$ gives $f'(-1)=12(-1)-10(-1)-6(1)=-12+10-6=-8$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the gradient is $-8$ **(A1)**. Because the gradient is negative, the function is decreasing at $x=-1$ **(R1)**. The negative gradient confirms the function falls there, just as it does at $x=1$, although the magnitude of the slope is larger. The negative gradient at both $x=1$ and $x=-1$ shows the curve is sloping downwards at those two points.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for rewriting $2/x^{3}$ as $2x^{-3}$ and differentiating each term with the power rule, (A1) for the three differentiated pieces, and (A1)(AG) for the combined derivative $12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$. The (R1) is for noting the negative index is retained. A candidate who writes $6/x^{4}$ instead of $-6x^{-4}$ loses the final mark. The negative index is the single most tested detail and must not be dropped.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$, (A1) for $12-10-6$, and (A1) for $-4$; the (R1) is for the negative gradient conclusion and its meaning for the slope of the curve.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=2$, (A1) for $96-20-6/16$, (A1) for $75.625$, and (R1) for noting the exact fractional subtraction. A candidate who rounds $6/16$ to $0.4$ earns the value mark only if the final answer is $75.6$. Exact arithmetic is expected at HL.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting $x=-1$, (A1) for $-12+10-6$, (A1) for $-8$, and (R1) for stating the function is decreasing because the gradient is negative. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed.
questions.explanation: This item drills the power rule when the index is a negative integer, the case the syllabus explicitly includes but students routinely mishandle. The function looks like a polynomial until the final term $2/x^{3}$, which must be rewritten as $2x^{-3}$ before differentiating; its derivative keeps a negative power, $-6x^{-4}$, rather than reverting to a fraction. The intended route is to differentiate each term separately, substitute the three given $x$-values, and interpret the sign of the resulting gradient. The gradient at $x=2$ is the trap: it is $96-20-6/16$, and the subtraction of $6/16=0.375$ must be carried out exactly to give $75.625$, a value that looks suspicious next to the tidy integers elsewhere. The classic wrong turn is to leave $2/x^{3}$ as a fraction and attempt the quotient rule, or to differentiate it as though the index were positive and write $+6x^{-4}$ or $-6x^{-2}$. Another error is to treat $x^{-4}$ at $x=2$ as $1/16$ but then add it instead of subtracting, giving $76.375$. Candidates also sometimes state that a negative gradient means the function is increasing, reversing the sign interpretation entirely. The numbers were chosen so that $x=1$ gives a clean $-4$, $x=-1$ gives $-8$, and only $x=2$ demands careful fraction arithmetic, isolating the negative-power skill and rewarding the candidate who keeps the algebra exact rather than approximate. The deliberate contrast between the three gradients is what makes the negative-power rule the unmistakable focus of the item. Keeping the algebra exact is the difference between the correct $75.625$ and a rounded error.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.3 bullet that the derivative of f(x)=ax^n is f'(x)=anx^{n-1} for integer n, including negative integer powers. The lever is the term 2/x^3, which must be rewritten as 2x^{-3} before differentiating and whose derivative keeps a negative power -6x^{-4}; the x-values 1, 2 and -1 were chosen so that the gradients are -4, the exact decimal 75.625 requiring careful subtraction of 6/16, and -8, isolating the negative-power rule. The item is not a reskin because the negative index must be retained rather than converted back to a fraction, and the fractional gradient at x=2 is the deliberate trap.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the derivative 12x^3-10x-6x^-4, its value -4 at x=1, its value 75.625 at x=2 from 96-20-6/16, its value -8 at x=-1, and the sign of that value being negative.
solution_skeleton: rewrite the reciprocal term as a negative power
differentiate term by term with the power rule
evaluate the derivative at the given point to obtain the gradient
use the gradient to find the tangent or normal required

questions.title: The tangent and normal to a curve that is not a polynomial
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.4 (tangents and normals at a given point, and their equations)
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Tangents and normals at a given point
questions.challenge_mechanism: The curve y=2x^2-3/x mixes a polynomial with a reciprocal, so the derivative 4x+3/x^2 must be evaluated at x=1 before the normal's negative reciprocal gradient is found.
questions.question: Consider the curve $y=2x^{2}-\frac{3}{x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x+\frac{3}{x^{2}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point on the curve where $x=1$ and the gradient of the curve there.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $x=1$.

questions.answer:
(a) Writing $\frac{3}{x}=3x^{-1}$, the derivative is $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x-(-3x^{-2})=4x+3x^{-2}=4x+\frac{3}{x^{2}}$ **(M1)(A1)(A1)(AG)**. The reciprocal term contributes $3x^{-2}$ because differentiating $-3x^{-1}$ raises the index from $-1$ to $-2$ and keeps the minus sign from the original term **(R1)**. The derivative is therefore confirmed as a sum of a polynomial part and a reciprocal part. This formula is the foundation for locating both the tangent and the normal.

(b) At $x=1$, the $y$-coordinate is $y=2(1)^{2}-\frac{3}{1}=2-3=-1$ **(M1)(A1)**, so the point on the curve is $(1,-1)$; the gradient there is $\frac{dy}{dx}=4(1)+\frac{3}{1^{2}}=4+3=7$ **(A1)**. The gradient is found by substituting $x=1$ into the derivative just established **(R1)**. The point and the gradient are therefore $(1,-1)$ and $7$, both of which are needed for the two line equations.

(c) Using the point-gradient form $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ with $m=7$ and $(1,-1)$ gives $y+1=7(x-1)$, which rearranges to $y=7x-8$ **(M1)(A1)**. The tangent shares the curve's gradient at the point of contact, so its slope is exactly $7$ **(A1)**. The equation is therefore $y=7x-8$, a line that just touches the curve at that single point **(R1)**.

(d) The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal $-\frac{1}{7}$ **(M1)(A1)**, and its equation is $y+1=-\frac{1}{7}(x-1)$, which simplifies to $y=-\frac{x}{7}-\frac{6}{7}$ **(A1)**. The normal's gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient, so their product is $-1$ **(R1)**. The equation is therefore $y=-\frac{x}{7}-\frac{6}{7}$, a line that cuts the curve at right angles at the point.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for rewriting $3/x$ as $3x^{-1}$ and differentiating, (A1) for the intermediate $4x+3x^{-2}$, and (A1)(AG) for the final $4x+3/x^{2}$. The (R1) is for explaining the sign of the reciprocal term. The sign must be positive for full marks; a candidate writing $-3/x^{2}$ loses the reasoning mark. The reciprocal contribution is the main trap and must be shown explicitly.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$ into $y$, (A1) for $y=-1$, (A1) for the gradient $7$ from the derivative, and (R1) for linking the gradient to the derivative. The point is $(1,-1)$. Both coordinates are required before either line can be written.

(c) Award (M1) for the point-gradient form, (A1) for $y+1=7(x-1)$, (A1) for $y=7x-8$, and (R1) for stating the tangent shares the curve's gradient. Accept equivalent forms such as $7x-y-8=0$.

(d) Award (M1) for the perpendicular gradient $-1/7$, (A1) for using point-gradient, (A1) for $y=-x/7-6/7$, and (R1) for the negative reciprocal property. Follow through from an incorrect gradient in (b) is allowed. Candidates who leave the answer in unsimplified point-gradient form earn the first two marks only.
questions.explanation: This item practises tangents and normals on a curve that is not a pure polynomial, because the term $-3/x$ forces the candidate to rewrite it as $-3x^{-1}$ before differentiating. The derivative becomes $4x+3/x^{2}$, and the whole problem turns on evaluating this correctly at $x=1$ to get the gradient $7$. The intended route is to differentiate, find the point $(1,-1)$, write the tangent with the same gradient using the point-gradient form, then take the negative reciprocal $-1/7$ for the normal. The trap is the reciprocal: differentiating $-3/x$ by eye tempts candidates to write $-3/x^{2}$ (forgetting the sign flip from the leading minus) or to apply the quotient rule and tangle the algebra. Another error is to confuse tangent and normal, using gradient $7$ for the normal or $-1/7$ for the tangent. The normal equation also needs careful rearrangement: $y+1=(-1/7)(x-1)$ expands to $y=-x/7+1/7-1=-x/7-6/7$, and candidates who stop at $y+1=-(x-1)/7$ without simplifying lose the final mark. The numbers were chosen so that $x=1$ gives tidy integers for the point and the tangent, isolating the reciprocal derivative as the only genuine difficulty; the normal then tests the negative-reciprocal rule on a clean fraction, and the negative $y$-coordinate must be carried carefully through both expansions. The combination of a reciprocal derivative with a fractional normal is what makes this more than a routine differentiation question. The blend of a reciprocal derivative with a fractional normal lifts this above a routine exercise, and the negative $y$-coordinate must be carried carefully through both line equations to avoid a sign slip.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.4 bullet on tangents and normals at a given point and their equations. The lever is the non-polynomial term -3/x in y=2x^2-3/x, which forces the candidate to rewrite it as -3x^{-1} and differentiate to 3/x^2; the point x=1 was chosen so the curve value is -1 and the gradient is the tidy integer 7, making the tangent y=7x-8 and the normal y=-x/7-6/7. The item is not a reskin because the reciprocal derivative and the negative-reciprocal gradient of the normal are the explicit difficulties, not the polynomial part.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the curve value y=-1 at x=1, the derivative 4x+3/x^2 at x=1 giving 7, the tangent y=7x-8 whose intercept at x=0 is -8, and the normal y=-x/7-6/7 whose intercept at x=0 is -6/7.
solution_skeleton: differentiate to obtain the gradient function
evaluate the gradient and the coordinate to form the tangent or normal
find where that line meets an axis or another curve
compute the required length or area from the intersection

questions.title: Rebuilding the function from its derivative and a single point
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.5 (introduction to integration as anti-differentiation of polynomial and exponential functions; the constant of integration)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The antiderivative 2x^3-2x^2+C is fixed by the single point f(1)=5, which pins C=5 and makes the definite integral equal the net change f(2)-f(1)=8.
questions.question: A function $f$ satisfies $f'(x)=6x^{2}-4x$ and $f(1)=5$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general antiderivative of $f'(x)$, including the constant of integration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of the constant of integration, given that $f(1)=5$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of the function when $x=2$.

questions.answer:
(a) Integrating $f'(x)=6x^{2}-4x$ term by term gives $f(x)=6\cdot\frac{x^{3}}{3}-4\cdot\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+C$ **(M1)(A1)**. The constant $C$ must be included because integration undoes differentiation only up to an additive constant **(A1)**. The general form is therefore $f(x)=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+C$, representing a whole family of parallel curves **(R1)**. The antiderivative is confirmed with the constant present, since any two antiderivatives differ only by a constant. This family picture is essential: without the condition in part (b) the exact curve cannot be singled out.

(b) Using the condition $f(1)=5$ gives $2(1)^{3}-2(1)^{2}+C=5$, so $2-2+C=5$ and therefore $C=5$ **(M1)(A1)**. The single data point pins down the otherwise free constant uniquely **(A1)**. The particular function is therefore $f(x)=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+5$ **(R1)**, the one member of the family that passes through $(1,5)$.

(c) With $C=5$ fixed, substituting $x=2$ gives $f(2)=2(8)-2(4)+5=16-8+5=13$ **(M1)(A1)**, so $f(2)=13$ **(A1)**. This value is found by substituting into the fully determined function, not by differentiating again **(R1)**. The value is therefore $13$, the height of the curve above the axis at that point.

(d) By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\int_{1}^{2}f'(x)\,dx=f(2)-f(1)$ **(M1)**, so this equals $13-5=8$ **(A1)**. Direct integration confirms it: $\int_{1}^{2}(6x^{2}-4x)\,dx=[2x^{3}-2x^{2}]_{1}^{2}=(16-8)-(2-2)=8$ **(A1)**, showing the two routes agree **(R1)**. The two methods agree, so the integral is $8$, which is exactly the net change in $f$ across the interval. Both the rebuilt function and the direct integral give the same number, which is the essence of the fundamental theorem.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for integrating each term of $6x^{2}-4x$, (A1) for $2x^{3}-2x^{2}$, (A1) for the constant $C$, and (R1) for noting an antiderivative needs the constant because differentiation erases it. A candidate who omits $C$ loses the constant mark but may earn the others. The constant is what distinguishes the family of solutions.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$ into the antiderivative, (A1) for $2-2+C=5$, (A1) for $C=5$, and (R1) for the idea that one point fixes the constant uniquely. Follow through from an incorrect antiderivative is allowed.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=2$, (A1) for $16-8+5$, (A1) for $13$, and (R1) for the interpretation that this is a function value, not a derivative. A candidate using the wrong $C$ forfeits only the final value if the method is sound.

(d) Award (M1) for the fundamental theorem $f(2)-f(1)$, (A1) for $13-5=8$, (A1) for the direct integration giving $8$, and (R1) for confirming the two methods agree. Both routes must be shown for full credit. Partial credit follows through from earlier errors in the antiderivative.
questions.explanation: This item reverses the usual direction of calculus: instead of differentiating, the candidate must rebuild $f$ from its derivative using anti-differentiation, then use a single known point to fix the constant. The derivative $6x^{2}-4x$ integrates cleanly to $2x^{3}-2x^{2}+C$, and the given condition $f(1)=5$ forces $C=5$ because the $x$-terms happen to cancel at $x=1$, leaving $C$ bare. The intended route is to integrate, substitute the point, evaluate $f(2)=13$, and finally observe that the definite integral of $f'$ from $1$ to $2$ equals the net change $f(2)-f(1)=8$. The classic wrong turn is to forget the constant of integration entirely, which makes part (b) impossible, or to write the antiderivative with the wrong power, such as $2x^{3}-4x^{2}$ by mishandling the $4x$ term. Another error is to evaluate $f(1)$ before integrating and treat it as the constant itself. In part (d) candidates sometimes compute the integral directly but fail to connect it to $f(2)-f(1)$, or they integrate $f$ instead of $f'$. The numbers were chosen so the $x$-terms cancel at $x=1$, isolating $C$, and so that $f(2)$ and the net change are small integers, keeping the focus on the method rather than on heavy arithmetic. The double appearance of the same antiderivative, once as the rebuilt function and once as the value of an integral, is the conceptual heart of the item and is the detail most often missed by candidates who treat the two parts as unrelated. The conceptual link between the rebuilt function and the integral of its derivative is the detail most often missed by strong candidates.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 5.5 bullet introducing integration as anti-differentiation of polynomial functions, including the constant of integration. The lever is the single condition f(1)=5 applied to the antiderivative of f'(x)=6x^2-4x; the coefficients were chosen so the antiderivative is 2x^3-2x^2+C and the x-terms cancel at x=1, leaving C=5 bare, then f(2)=13 and the definite integral equals the net change f(2)-f(1)=8. The item is not a reskin because the constant must be determined from one point and the final part requires recognising the integral of f' as the net change, reversing the usual differentiation direction.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the general antiderivative 2x^3-2x^2+C, the condition f(1)=5 giving 2-2+5=5, the value f(2)=16-8+5=13, the derivative 6x^2-4x at x=2 giving 16, and the net change 2(1)^3-2(1)^2=0.

evaluate the function at the argument required

questions.title: A logarithmic inequality proved from the sign of a derivative
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.6 (derivative of x^n, n in Q; derivative of sin x, cos x, e^x and ln x); AHL 5.13 (evaluation of limits)
questions.subtopic: 5.6 Derivative of x^n, sin x, cos x, e^x and ln x
questions.challenge_mechanism: The derivative collapses to a perfect square over a positive denominator, so the sign of the difference function is settled without ever locating a turning point, and the inequality reverses at x = 1 because the function is increasing and vanishes there. The limit part then exposes that a bound can be exact at one point and useless at infinity.
questions.question: For $x>0$, define $\displaystyle h(x)=\ln x-\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}$. The four parts below use the derivative of $h$ to compare $\ln x$ with a rational function of $x$, and then ask whether that comparison is worth much once $x$ is large.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $h(1)=0$, and show that $\displaystyle h'(x)=\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{x(x+1)^{2}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that $h'(x)\ge 0$ for every $x>0$. Hence determine, giving a reason in each case, which of $\ln x$ and $\dfrac{2(x-1)}{x+1}$ is the larger when $x>1$ and when $0<x<1$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty} h(x)$, and hence comment on whether the comparison established in part (b) gives a useful bound on $\ln x$ for large values of $x$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence, without using a calculator, determine which of $\ln 2$ and $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is the larger, justifying your answer.

questions.answer:
**(a)** $h(1)=\ln 1-\dfrac{2(1-1)}{1+1}=0-0=0$. **(A1)** For the derivative, differentiate the rational term by the quotient rule:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}\right)=\frac{2(x+1)-2(x-1)}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{4}{(x+1)^{2}}$$ **(M1)(A1)**
so, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln x=\dfrac{1}{x}$, **(M1)**
$$h'(x)=\frac{1}{x}-\frac{4}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{(x+1)^{2}-4x}{x(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{x^{2}-2x+1}{x(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{x(x+1)^{2}}$$ **(A1)(AG)**
The numerator completes to a perfect square, which is the fact the rest of the question depends on.

**(b)** For $x>0$ we have $x>0$ and $(x+1)^{2}>0$, so the denominator $x(x+1)^{2}$ is positive, while $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for every real $x$. Hence $h'(x)\ge 0$ on the whole domain, with equality only at $x=1$. **(M1)(A1)** Therefore $h$ is increasing on $(0,\infty)$. **(R1)** Since $h(1)=0$, it follows that
$$x>1 \Rightarrow h(x)>0 \Rightarrow \ln x>\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1},\qquad 0<x<1 \Rightarrow h(x)<0 \Rightarrow \ln x<\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}.$$ **(A1)(A1)**
The inequality reverses at $x=1$, and that reversal is the point: the two expressions are equal at $x=1$ and the comparison changes direction there rather than holding one way throughout.

**(c)** As $x\to\infty$, the rational term satisfies $\dfrac{2(x-1)}{x+1}=\dfrac{2-2/x}{1+1/x}\to 2$, whereas $\ln x\to\infty$. **(M1)(A1)** Hence $h(x)\to\infty$. **(A1)** The bound is therefore true but increasingly weak: it never exceeds $2$, so for large $x$ it says only that $\ln x$ is bigger than a quantity that has stopped growing. **(R1)** What makes the inequality interesting is the opposite end. At $x=1$ the two sides are equal and, since $h'(1)=0$, their first derivatives agree as well, so near $x=1$ the rational expression approximates $\ln x$ to second order and the bound is excellent; the same statement degrades steadily as $x$ moves away from $1$.

**(d)** Put $x=2$, which is greater than $1$, so the first case of part (b) applies: **(M1)**
$$\ln 2>\frac{2(2-1)}{2+1}=\frac{2}{3}.$$ **(A1)**
Hence $\ln 2$ is the larger of the two. **(A1)** No decimal value is needed, and none is available without a calculator, which is exactly why the inequality is worth having; the conclusion is rigorous even though the gap is only about $0.026$. **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) The quotient rule must be shown rather than quoted, because the simplification to a single square is where the mark is earned. Award (A1) for $4/(x+1)^{2}$ and do not accept an unsimplified $\big[(x+1)^{2}-4x\big]$ numerator as final. (b) The sign argument must name both factors: positivity of the denominator and non-negativity of the square. A candidate who says only 'the derivative is positive' has skipped the case $x=1$ and should not receive the final mark. Award the reversal in full only if both directions are given; a candidate who states the $x>1$ case alone has done half the question. (c) Accept any correct evaluation of the limit; the comment mark is for noticing that a bound that tends to $2$ cannot track a function that tends to infinity. Credit the observation about agreement of value and gradient at $x=1$ as an alternative acceptable comment. (d) The word 'hence' is load-bearing: the mark is for substituting $x=2$ into the part (b) result, not for quoting a decimal for $\ln 2$. A candidate who writes $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$ and compares has not answered the question as set and should be credited only for the conclusion.
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a move that students meet early and rarely see used seriously: if a function is increasing and you know its value at one point, you know an inequality everywhere. Nothing here needs a turning point. The derivative of $h$ happens to be a perfect square divided by a quantity that is positive on the whole domain, so its sign is settled by inspection, and because $h(1)=0$ the sign of $h$ itself follows immediately on either side of $1$. The result is a clean comparison between a logarithm and a rational function, obtained without evaluating anything.

The detail that makes the item worth sixteen marks is the reversal. Students expect an inequality proved by monotonicity to hold in one direction throughout, and here it does not: the two expressions are equal at $x=1$ and the comparison swaps over. A candidate who establishes $h'(x)\ge 0$ and then reports a single direction has done the hard part and then thrown away the most interesting consequence. This is why part (b) asks for both cases explicitly.

Part (c) is included because a proved inequality is not automatically a useful one, and judging usefulness is a separate skill from proving. The rational bound tends to $2$, so it cannot possibly track a function that grows without limit; the inequality is exact at $x=1$, excellent nearby, and steadily less informative as $x$ grows. Part (d) then puts the inequality to work in the one situation where it is at its best: comparing $\ln 2$ with $2/3$ is a question about a number close to $1$, and it can be settled rigorously with no calculator at all. The genre is a standard one in Chinese school mathematics, where inequalities of the form $\ln x \gtrless 2(x-1)/(x+1)$ are proved by exactly this square-over-positive-denominator argument, and it transfers cleanly to IB command terms because the reasoning is short enough to write out in full.

There is a broader lesson in the structure. Proving an inequality by differentiating a carefully chosen auxiliary function is a technique that appears across the syllabus, and the auxiliary function here is chosen so that its derivative factorises as a square. Recognising that a derivative *might* do that, and choosing the function accordingly, is the transferable skill; the particular inequality is not.

Context, numbers and command terms are IB-specific.

verification.method: h(1), the closed form of h'(x), the sign argument and the numerical comparisons were all recomputed in Python to full precision; h'(x) was additionally checked against a central-difference approximation of h at nine points spanning 0.25 to 100.
solution_skeleton: differentiate the logarithmic term and the rational term and combine them over a common denominator
complete the square in the numerator so the derivative is a square over a positive quantity
deduce the sign of the difference function from the sign of its derivative together with one known value
compare the growth of the logarithmic and rational parts in the limit to judge whether the bound is sharp
apply the inequality at a particular value to compare two numbers without a calculator

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Look for a turning point of the difference function, locate the minimum, and read the inequality off the value of the function there.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The derivative is a perfect square over a quantity that is positive on the whole domain, so the sign is settled by inspection and no turning point is ever needed; the value at x = 1 does all the work, and the comparison changes direction across it.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A single inequality direction carried across the whole domain, with the sign of the difference asserted rather than deduced from monotonicity and one known value.
